raw_response:
I’m 53 this year, and I’ve worked this land long enough to know that steady yield matters more than chasing the absolute maximum. On my 12 mu, I’ll keep the wheat-maize rotation the same. It fits our land, our labor, and our water situation. I have well irrigation, so I’m not as exposed as people who wait only on rain, but pumping costs money, so I still won’t irrigate carelessly. Since I have some education and many years of experience, I look at both what worked on my own fields and what the better farmers around Quzhou are doing. Last year, when wheat had enough base fertilizer and one timely topdress, the stand stayed even. Maize also does best when I plant immediately after wheat harvest and don’t lose moisture.

For wheat, I’ll sow in early October with an improved local variety, not the cheapest seed but not the most expensive either. I want a stable stand and good overwintering. I’ll put most phosphorus and potassium in as base fertilizer, with part of the nitrogen at sowing and the rest at jointing. Wheat is the crop where I’m less willing to save too much on fertilizer, because if it turns yellow in spring, yield loss comes fast. I expect to irrigate about three times if rainfall is normal: once after sowing if soil is dry, once around jointing, and once around grain filling depending on weather. For maize, the main thing is speed after wheat harvest. I’ll use a hybrid and plant within a few days after wheat comes off. I won’t do heavy tillage because the turnaround is too tight; I’ll use simple residue handling and quick sowing. I’ll apply base fertilizer at planting and then topdress nitrogen around the big flare stage. If summer rain is decent, maybe I only irrigate once, but if it turns dry, I’ll give a second watering. I’d rather spend a bit on one timely irrigation than lose ear size later.
